Literal Interpretation

The Famine and Divine Prohibition

Genesis 26 opens with a famine striking the land, distinct from the earlier famine in Abraham's time: "And there came a famine in the country, besides that famine which had happened in the days of Abraham. And Isaac went to Abimelech king of the Philistines to Gerara" (Gen 26:1). The land of Canaan was prone to periodic droughts, and Isaac naturally considered following his father's example by descending into Egypt, the land of abundant water from the Nile.

Yet God intervenes with a direct prohibition: "Go not down into Egypt, but stay in the land that I shall tell thee. And sojourn in this land, and I will be with thee, and will bless thee" (Gen 26:2-3). This divine command distinguishes Isaac's situation from Abraham's. While Abraham had gone to Egypt during famine, Isaac is commanded to remain in the promised land, demonstrating that God's providence can sustain His servants even amid scarcity.

St. Augustine, in his Questions on Genesis, addresses the question of whether the Abimelech in Genesis 26 could be the same ruler as in Abraham's time:

"Suppose Abimelech was a young man when he desired Sarah and became friends with Abraham. He could, therefore, be almost a hundred years old when Isaac encountered him. Nothing obliges us to think Isaac's departure for Gerar is reported by way of recapitulation."

St. Augustine, Questions on Genesis

Many commentators suggest that "Abimelech" was a dynastic title rather than a personal name, similar to "Pharaoh" in Egypt. This would explain the presence of rulers bearing this name across different generations.

Isaac's Deception Concerning Rebekah

Despite receiving God's promise of protection and blessing, Isaac falls into the same fearful deception as his father Abraham. When the men of Gerar inquire about the beautiful Rebekah, Isaac claims: "She is my sister. For he was afraid to confess that she was his wife, thinking lest perhaps they would kill him because of her beauty" (Gen 26:7).

The deception is discovered when Abimelech observes Isaac's intimate behavior with Rebekah: "And when many days were passed, and he abode there, Abimelech king of the Philistines looking out through a window, saw him playing with Rebecca his wife" (Gen 26:8). The Hebrew word used here, metsacheq, shares the same root as Isaac's name and carries the sense of jesting, laughing, or caressing in a manner appropriate only between husband and wife.

Abimelech's rebuke is sharp and justified: "Why hast thou deceived us? Some man of the people might have lain with thy wife, and thou hadst brought upon us a great sin" (Gen 26:10). The pagan king recognizes the gravity of adultery more clearly than the patriarch had anticipated. Augustine notes in his City of God, Book XVI, that while he undertakes to justify Abraham and consequently Isaac in their precaution, the Holy Spirit recorded Abimelech's reproof, and we ought to admit its equity.

The Hundredfold Blessing

Despite Isaac's moral failure, God's promise of blessing is fulfilled abundantly: "And Isaac sowed in that land, and he found that same year a hundredfold: and the Lord blessed him. And the man was enriched, and he went on prospering and increasing, till he became exceeding great" (Gen 26:12-13). A hundredfold return on agricultural investment was extraordinarily rare in the ancient Near East, signifying unmistakable divine favor.

Augustine comments on the relationship between earthly prosperity and divine blessing:

"Scripture says about Isaac 'the Lord blessed him. And the man was exalted, and advancing he increased, till he became very great.' Although this means something spiritual, even these temporary goods can only be given by God and should only be expected from him."

St. Augustine, Questions on Genesis

The Philistines' response to Isaac's prosperity was envy rather than gratitude: "And the Philistines envied him, and stopped up at that time all the wells, that the servants of his father Abraham had digged, filling them up with earth" (Gen 26:14-15). This destructive act was particularly malicious in an arid land where water sources were essential for survival.

The Wells of Isaac

After Abimelech asks Isaac to depart because of his growing power, Isaac moves to the valley of Gerara and begins to re-dig the wells that Abraham's servants had dug. The narrative of the three named wells forms the heart of the chapter:

"And he digged also other wells, which the servants of his father Abraham had digged, and which, after his death, the Philistines had stopped up: and he called them by the same names, by which his father before had called them" (Gen 26:18). Isaac's act of restoring his father's wells and preserving their original names demonstrates both filial piety and continuity with Abraham's covenant.

The first well discovered by Isaac's servants produced "living water" (aquam vivam), meaning fresh, flowing spring water rather than stagnant cistern water. Yet the herdsmen of Gerara claimed it, so "he called the name of the well, on occasion of that which had happened, Calumny" (Gen 26:20). The Hebrew name Esek means "contention" or "dispute."

The second well met with similar opposition: "And they digged also another; and for that also they quarrelled, and he called the name of it, Enmity" (Gen 26:21). The Hebrew name Sitnah derives from the same root as "Satan" and means "hostility" or "accusation."

Only with the third well does peace arrive: "Going forward from thence, he digged another well, for which they contended not: therefore he called the name thereof, Latitude, saying: Now hath the Lord given us room, and made us to increase upon the earth" (Gen 26:22). The Hebrew name Rehoboth means "broad places" or "spaciousness," signifying the end of conflict and the beginning of undisturbed prosperity.

The Theophany at Beersheba

Isaac proceeds to Beersheba, the site associated with his father's covenant with Abimelech. There God appears to him: "And the Lord appeared to him that same night, saying: I am the God of Abraham thy father, fear not, for I am with thee: I will bless thee, and multiply thy seed for my servant Abraham's sake" (Gen 26:24). This theophany confirms the continuity of the Abrahamic covenant and encourages Isaac after his experiences of conflict.

Isaac responds appropriately: "And he built there an altar: and called upon the name of the Lord, and pitched his tent; and commanded his servants to dig a well" (Gen 26:25). The three actions of building an altar, calling upon the Lord, and establishing a permanent settlement with water supply demonstrate Isaac's faithful response to divine assurance.

The Covenant with Abimelech

Abimelech arrives with his adviser Ochozath and his general Phicol, seeking a covenant with Isaac. When Isaac questions their motives, given their previous hostility, they respond: "We saw that the Lord is with thee, and therefore we said: Let there be an oath between us, and let us make a covenant" (Gen 26:28). The visible blessing of God upon Isaac has transformed enemies into those seeking alliance.

The covenant meal and oath-swearing follow ancient Near Eastern custom: "And he made them a feast, and after they had eaten and drunk: Arising in the morning, they swore one to another" (Gen 26:30-31). The timing of the servants' report about finding water coincides with the departure of Abimelech's delegation, leading Isaac to name the well Shebah ("oath"), giving the place its name Beersheba ("well of the oath").

Esau's Hittite Wives

The chapter concludes with a jarring note: "And Esau being forty years old, married wives, Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hethite, and Basemath the daughter of Elon of the same place: And they both offended the mind of Isaac and Rebecca" (Gen 26:34-35). Esau's marriage to Hittite women violated the principle that Abraham had established when he sought a wife for Isaac from among his own kindred rather than from the Canaanites.

The grief caused to Isaac and Rebekah by these marriages provides important context for the events of the following chapter. Esau's lack of spiritual discernment in marriage parallels his earlier sale of his birthright, demonstrating a pattern of valuing immediate gratification over covenantal responsibility.

Allegorical Interpretation

Isaac as Figure of Christ

The Church Fathers consistently saw Isaac as a type of Christ, and the events of Genesis 26 continue this typological reading. As Origen observed, Isaac's very name, meaning "laughter" or "joy," prophesied the joy that Christ would bring to humanity. The parallels extend throughout Isaac's life: his miraculous birth to aged parents, his role as the beloved son, his willing submission at the Akedah, and now his patient endurance amid persecution.

St. Ambrose, in his treatise De Isaac et Anima (On Isaac and the Soul), develops an extended allegory in which Isaac represents Christ, and his encounters at the wells symbolize the relationship between the Word and the soul:

"Isaac is 'verus Isaac' - an archetype of Christ. The wisdom of Scripture is presented as the source and end of all knowledge, and the soul is shown on the difficult path of perfection, in relation to the Word. By depicting Christ as present in history and in the figure of Isaac, Ambrose invites all those who come to listen to him - as if they were this soul - to the true heart of the mystery of Christ."

Traditional patristic commentary on Ambrose's De Isaac et Anima

The Wells as Sources of Divine Wisdom

Origen devoted his thirteenth Homily on Genesis to the allegorical interpretation of Isaac's wells. For Origen, the wells represent the Scriptures, and the act of digging represents the spiritual labor of interpreting them correctly. The Philistines who fill the wells with earth symbolize those who obstruct access to spiritual truth through carnal or erroneous interpretation:

"So, therefore, the wells which Abraham dug, that is the Scriptures of the Old Testament, have been filled with earth by the Philistines, or evil teachers, Scribes and Pharisees, or even hostile powers; and their veins have been stopped up lest they provide a drink for those who are of Abraham."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis, Homily XIII

Christ, the true Isaac, comes to reopen these wells and restore access to the living water of divine wisdom. Origen continues:

"For that people cannot drink from the Scriptures, but suffer a 'thirst for the word of God,' until Isaac should come and open them that his servants may drink. Thanks, therefore, to Christ, the son of Abraham, who has come and opened the wells for us. For he opened them for those men who said: 'Was not our heart burning in us when he opened to us the Scriptures?'"

Origen, Homilies on Genesis, Homily XIII

The reference to Luke 24:32, where the disciples on the road to Emmaus speak of their hearts burning as Jesus opened the Scriptures to them, demonstrates how Origen sees Isaac's well-digging as prefiguring Christ's interpretive ministry.

The Three Named Wells

The progression of the three wells - Esek (Contention), Sitnah (Enmity), and Rehoboth (Broad Places) - has been understood as tracing the soul's journey toward spiritual peace, or as representing the history of salvation:

Origen's allegorical interpretation sees the wells as stages in the acquisition of spiritual knowledge:

"If I shall wish to dig deeply and open the hidden veins of living water, immediately the Philistines will be present and will strive with me. They will stir up disputes and malicious charges against me and will begin to refill my wells with their earth and mud."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis

According to this reading, those who seek to understand Scripture deeply will face opposition from worldly forces that prefer to keep spiritual truth buried. The wells represent successively deeper levels of understanding: the literal sense meets with contention from those who deny its validity; the moral sense encounters enmity from those who resist its demands; but the spiritual sense, when finally attained, opens into the broad places of divine contemplation where there is room enough for all.

Medieval Jewish commentators, whose interpretations often parallel patristic ones, saw the three wells as representing the three Temples of Jerusalem. The first Temple, built by Solomon, was destroyed through contention with the Babylonians. The second Temple fell through the hostility of the Romans. The third Temple, to be built by the Messiah, will endure forever in peace. Christian interpreters adapted this schema to represent the progression from the synagogue (rejected) to the Church militant (persecuted) to the Church triumphant (vindicated).

Living Water and Baptism

The discovery of "living water" (aqua viva) in Isaac's wells prefigures the sacrament of baptism and the gift of the Holy Spirit. The Gospel of John uses this same terminology when Jesus speaks to the Samaritan woman: "If thou didst know the gift of God, and who he is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou perhaps wouldst have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water" (Jn 4:10).

The Church Fathers consistently connected the Old Testament well narratives with baptismal theology. The living water that springs from the earth, in contrast to stagnant cistern water, represents the vivifying grace that flows from Christ through the sacraments. As one patristic synthesis states:

"When Jesus says to the Samaritan woman, 'I'm going to give you living water,' he's not just talking about H2O. He's talking about the waters of baptism through which we receive the living water of the Holy Spirit. Baptism in Jesus makes us 'walking wells' for our own thirst and the thirst of others."

Traditional patristic interpretation

Isaac and Rebekah as Christ and the Church

Ambrose's De Isaac et Anima develops an extended bridal mysticism in which Isaac and Rebekah represent Christ and the faithful soul, or Christ and the Church. The encounter between them, interpreted through the lens of the Song of Songs, becomes an allegory of the soul's union with the divine Word:

"In this interpretation, the couple of Isaac and Rebecca serve as models of the couple formed by Christ and the soul. Ambrose interprets their encounter through the prism of the Song of Songs and in relation to the wells that Isaac digs. Rebecca evolves from a historical figure to a representation of the soul, illustrating the ideal Christian path through her relationship with Isaac."

Summary of Ambrose's De Isaac et Anima

The Covenant as Figure of the New Covenant

The covenant between Isaac and Abimelech at Beersheba prefigures the peace that Christ establishes between God and humanity, and between formerly hostile peoples. The Philistines, representing the Gentile nations, recognize that God is with Isaac and seek alliance with him. So too the Gentiles, recognizing Christ, are incorporated into the covenant people through faith.

The oath at Beersheba ("Well of the Oath") points to the baptismal covenant in which believers swear fidelity to Christ. The meal shared between Isaac and Abimelech's party prefigures the Eucharistic feast that seals the New Covenant.

Esau's Wives and Spiritual Adultery

Esau's marriage to Hittite women, which grieved Isaac and Rebekah, allegorically represents the soul that abandons the true faith to unite itself with worldly error. Just as Esau chose wives from among the Canaanites rather than from the covenant family, so those who forsake sound doctrine to embrace heresy or worldliness commit spiritual adultery against the Lord.

The contrast between Esau's hasty, self-willed marriages and the careful seeking of a bride for Isaac (Genesis 24) illustrates the difference between the carnal and the spiritual man. Esau, born first according to the flesh, lives according to the flesh and makes choices that grieve the Spirit. Isaac, the child of promise, acts in accordance with the covenant and receives God's blessing.
moral:
Moral (Tropological) Interpretation

Obedience in the Midst of Famine

When famine struck the land, Isaac's natural inclination was to follow his father's example and seek provision in Egypt. Yet God commanded him to remain in the land of promise: "Go not down into Egypt, but stay in the land that I shall tell thee" (Gen 26:2). Isaac's obedience to this counterintuitive command models the virtue of faith that trusts God's word over human prudence.

The moral lesson is clear: God's provision is not limited by natural circumstances. While Egypt seemed the reasonable choice for survival, God intended to demonstrate His power to sustain Isaac even in famine. As Augustine observed regarding Isaac's subsequent prosperity:

"Although this means something spiritual, even these temporary goods can only be given by God and should only be expected from him."

St. Augustine, Questions on Genesis

Christians today face similar tests when worldly wisdom suggests one course of action while God's word points another way. The path of obedience may seem foolish or dangerous, but God honors those who trust His promises.

The Sin of Fear-Driven Deception

Despite receiving divine assurance, Isaac fell into the same sinful pattern as his father Abraham, deceiving Abimelech about his relationship with Rebekah. This teaches us that even those who have received God's promises remain susceptible to fear-driven sin. Isaac had been told explicitly that God would bless and protect him, yet he still feared for his life and resorted to deception.

The rebuke from Abimelech should humble us: a pagan king recognized the gravity of the potential sin more clearly than the patriarch. This reminds us that conscience and natural law are written on every human heart, and that unbelievers sometimes display better moral judgment than believers who have been compromised by fear or self-interest.

The moral application is sobering: past spiritual experiences and present divine promises do not exempt us from the ongoing struggle with sin. We must continually bring our fears to God rather than addressing them through deception or manipulation.

The Virtue of Patience Under Provocation

The narrative of Isaac's wells provides a masterclass in patient endurance. When the Philistines stopped up his father's wells with earth, Isaac simply dug new ones. When the herdsmen of Gerara claimed the first well, Isaac named it "Contention" and moved on. When they disputed the second well, he named it "Enmity" and moved on again. Only at the third well did he find peace.

St. John Chrysostom extolled Isaac's patience as exemplary virtue:

"Isaac was stronger, and this is why God left him alone, so as to increase his patience."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis

Isaac had the power to fight for his rights. The text notes that Abimelech asked him to leave precisely because "thou art become mightier than we" (Gen 26:16). Yet Isaac chose peace over conflict, moving away rather than asserting his legitimate claims by force. This demonstrates the virtue of meekness - not weakness, but strength under control.

Chrysostom elsewhere teaches the value of patience in adversity:

"Isaac neither reproached her nor fell into despair. This reveals his patience and moderation, as well as his great forbearance."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis

Perseverance in Good Works

The Philistines' malicious destruction of Abraham's wells did not deter Isaac from the labor of digging anew. Three times he dug wells; three times he faced opposition. But he persevered until he found Rehoboth, "Broad Places," where there was room enough for all. The moral lesson is that righteous work will eventually be vindicated, even if it must pass through periods of contention and enmity.

Origen encouraged believers to persist in the spiritual labor of seeking divine wisdom despite opposition:

"Observe each detail which has been written. For, if one knows how to dig into the depth, he will find a treasure in the details, and perhaps also, the precious jewels of the mysteries lie hidden where they are not esteemed."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis

The Christian life requires this same perseverance. We may face opposition, misunderstanding, and repeated setbacks, but we must continue digging into Scripture, prayer, and good works until we find the living water that satisfies.

The Blessing of Peacemaking

Isaac's commitment to peace ultimately brought his enemies to seek reconciliation. Abimelech, who had expelled Isaac from his territory, came to Beersheba seeking covenant: "We saw that the Lord is with thee" (Gen 26:28). Isaac's refusal to retaliate, combined with God's obvious blessing upon him, convinced even his adversaries that alliance was preferable to continued conflict.

Our Lord teaches: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God" (Mt 5:9). Isaac's example shows that genuine peacemaking is not passive avoidance of conflict but active pursuit of reconciliation, even at personal cost. The feast that Isaac prepared for Abimelech's delegation and the mutual oath-swearing demonstrate the concrete steps necessary to transform enmity into friendship.

The Grief of Imprudent Marriage

The chapter concludes with the sorrow caused to Isaac and Rebekah by Esau's marriages to Hittite women. This teaches the importance of marital choice for the spiritual wellbeing of the entire family. Esau's decision was made without consultation, without regard for covenantal identity, and without consideration for his parents' wishes.

The grief experienced by Isaac and Rebekah warns parents and children alike: marriage is not merely a personal choice but a family and covenantal matter. Those who marry outside the faith, or who marry hastily without wise counsel, bring sorrow upon themselves and their families. Conversely, those who seek spouses from among the faithful, with proper discernment and family involvement, build households that honor God.

Gratitude and Worship

After the theophany at Beersheba, Isaac's first response was worship: "And he built there an altar: and called upon the name of the Lord" (Gen 26:25). This pattern of responding to divine encounter with worship provides a model for the Christian life. Every blessing, every deliverance, every word from God should prompt us to build an altar of thanksgiving.

Isaac's worship was not private but public, involving the construction of a visible altar and the invocation of God's name. This teaches that our gratitude should not remain hidden but should be expressed in ways that bear witness to God's goodness before others. The Philistines who later came seeking peace had perhaps witnessed Isaac's devotion and recognized in it the source of his blessing.

Anagogical Interpretation

The Land of Promise and the Heavenly Country

God's command to Isaac - "Go not down into Egypt, but stay in the land that I shall tell thee" (Gen 26:2) - has profound eschatological significance. Egypt, representing the world with its fleshly abundance, stands in contrast to the promised land, which, though presently afflicted by famine, is the inheritance given by God. Isaac's choice to remain in Canaan despite hardship prefigures the Christian's choice to endure temporal difficulties rather than abandon the hope of eternal inheritance.

The Letter to the Hebrews interprets the patriarchal sojourning in eschatological terms: "All these died according to faith, not having received the promises, but beholding them afar off... and confessing that they are pilgrims and strangers on the earth. For they that say these things, do signify that they seek a country" (Heb 11:13-14). Isaac's dwelling in Canaan as a stranger, moving from place to place, digging wells but never settling permanently, images the Christian pilgrimage toward the heavenly homeland.

The Wells of Living Water and Eternal Life

The "living water" (aqua viva) discovered in Isaac's wells points ultimately to the eternal springs of paradise. Origen's interpretation connects the patriarchal wells with the heavenly reality:

"If one knows how to dig into the depth, he will find a treasure in the details, and perhaps also, the precious jewels of the mysteries lie hidden where they are not esteemed."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis

The Apocalypse describes the final fulfillment: "And he showed me a river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb" (Rev 22:1). The wells that sustained Isaac in the wilderness of Gerara were foretastes of this eternal fountain. Every drink of living water in this life is a pledge of the inexhaustible refreshment that awaits the saints.

The progression from Esek (Contention) through Sitnah (Enmity) to Rehoboth (Broad Places) traces the journey of the Church and the individual soul from present tribulation to eternal peace. In this age, we face contention and enmity; in the age to come, God will make room for us in the broad places of His kingdom.

Rehoboth and the New Jerusalem

Isaac's naming of the third well Rehoboth with the declaration "Now hath the Lord given us room, and made us to increase upon the earth" (Gen 26:22) anticipates the spaciousness of the heavenly city. The New Jerusalem, as described in Revelation 21, is of vast dimensions - twelve thousand stadia in each direction - signifying that there is room for all the redeemed.

St. Augustine's teaching on the heavenly Jerusalem applies here:

"Fitly, therefore, does Isaac, the child of promise, typify the children of grace, the citizens of the free city."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XV

The children of Isaac, born according to the Spirit, are destined for citizenship in this city where there will be no more contention, no more enmity, but only the broad places of eternal fellowship with God and His saints.

The Hundredfold Blessing and Heavenly Reward

Isaac's hundredfold harvest in the midst of famine (Gen 26:12) prefigures the superabundant reward promised to the faithful. Our Lord uses precisely this imagery in His teaching: "And every one that hath left house, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands for my name's sake, shall receive an hundredfold, and shall possess life everlasting" (Mt 19:29).

The hundredfold is not merely quantitative increase but qualitative transformation. What is sown in the corruption of this age will be reaped in the incorruption of the resurrection. Isaac's exceptional harvest amid scarcity images the paradox of Christian hope: those who seem to have nothing in this world possess the promise of everything in the world to come.

The Covenant of Peace

The covenant that Abimelech sought with Isaac - a covenant of mutual non-aggression, sealed with an oath and a feast - points toward the eternal peace that God will establish in the final age. The prophet Ezekiel speaks of this ultimate covenant: "And I will make a covenant of peace with them, it shall be an everlasting covenant with them" (Ez 37:26).

In this present age, the Church militant faces opposition and persecution, as Isaac faced the contention of the Philistines. But a day is coming when all enemies will be reconciled or subdued, when the knowledge of God will cover the earth as waters cover the sea. The peace that Isaac experienced at Rehoboth, and the covenant he established with Abimelech, are foretastes of this eschatological reality.

The Theophany and the Beatific Vision

God's appearance to Isaac at Beersheba - "I am the God of Abraham thy father, fear not, for I am with thee" (Gen 26:24) - was a partial revelation, a word in the night. But it points toward the full vision of God that awaits the blessed. As St. John writes: "We shall see him as he is" (1 Jn 3:2).

The theophanies of the Old Testament were accommodations to human weakness, veiled manifestations of the divine glory. But in the heavenly Jerusalem, "they shall see his face: and his name shall be on their foreheads" (Rev 22:4). What Isaac knew by faith, the saints will know by sight; what he received as promise, they will possess as fulfillment.

The Separation of Esau and the Final Judgment

Esau's marriages to Hittite women, which "offended the mind of Isaac and Rebecca" (Gen 26:35), foreshadow the final separation between those within the covenant and those outside. Esau, who despised his birthright and united himself with the Canaanites, represents those who exchange their eternal inheritance for temporal pleasure.

The Apostle Paul warns: "Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau; who for one mess, sold his first birthright. For know ye that afterwards, when he desired to inherit the benediction, he was rejected; for he found no place of repentance, although with tears he had sought it" (Heb 12:16-17). The grief of Isaac and Rebekah over Esau's marriages anticipates the sorrow of the final judgment, when those who chose the world over the kingdom will be excluded from the inheritance of the saints.

Beersheba and the Eternal Sabbath

The name Beersheba, "Well of the Oath," carries eschatological significance. The oath sworn there between Isaac and Abimelech was a covenant of peace, and the well provided water for life. In the heavenly Beersheba, God's oath of salvation is eternally fulfilled, and the living water flows forever.

Isaac's settlement at Beersheba, where he built an altar, called upon God, pitched his tent, and dug a well, represents the fourfold fullness of the eternal state: worship before God's throne, intimate communion with the divine name, dwelling in God's presence, and partaking of the water of life. What Isaac established temporarily and symbolically, the saints will enjoy permanently and truly in the kingdom that cannot be shaken.

The Letter to the Hebrews teaches: "There remaineth therefore a day of rest for the people of God" (Heb 4:9). Isaac's rest at Beersheba, after the contention and enmity of his earlier sojourning, prefigures the eternal Sabbath when all striving will cease and the people of God will enter fully into the rest promised to them from the foundation of the world.
